title: Architecture for a large app and many teams
summary: When 50-200 engineers ship one iOS app, the architecture is mostly about boundaries: modules with owners, a thin app shell, shared platform services, fast builds, and guardrails that keep the main branch releasable.
requirements: Teams ship features independently without stepping on each other.
Build and CI times stay low as the codebase grows.
Consistent quality: performance budgets, accessibility, analytics conventions.
components: App shell: composition root, navigation router, feature registration
Feature modules with interface/implementation split and demo apps
Platform modules: networking, persistence, design system, analytics, flags, logging
Build tooling: SPM or Bazel/Tuist, remote cache, module graph linting
Governance: CODEOWNERS, RFC/ADR process, architecture review
tradeoffs: More modules give better isolation and incremental builds but add link time, indexing load and boilerplate.
Central platform team ensures consistency but can become a bottleneck; enable contributions with clear standards.
Bazel gives hermetic, cached builds at scale but adds tooling complexity versus SPM/Xcode.
body: **Boundaries:** features communicate through interface modules and the router, never by importing each other's implementation. Shared state goes through platform services with explicit APIs.
**Guardrails in CI:** dependency rules, app size and launch-time budgets, snapshot tests for design-system components, lint for analytics event schemas, mandatory feature flags for new features.
**Migration story:** extract platform modules first (networking, design system), then carve features starting from the most-changed code, keeping the app shippable every week.

**Staff signals:** measure (build time, PR cycle time, crash rate by module), write the RFC, get buy-in across teams, provide tooling (module generator), and define deprecation paths for old patterns.
